label: Spreading with anchors and pseudo-nets
lesson:
# Spreading with anchors and pseudo-nets

A quadratic placement solution is wirelength-optimal and hopelessly overlapped. Spreading turns it into a distributed placement. Modern quadratic placers such as SimPL compute a spread-out target for every cell and pull cells toward it with anchor pseudo-nets, solving the linear system again, so that wirelength and density are traded gradually over many iterations.

## Anchors as extra fixed pins

An anchor is a pseudo-net, a two-pin connection of weight $\alpha$ from a movable cell to a fixed point at its target position $t$. To the linear system it is just another fixed connection: it adds $\alpha$ to the cell's diagonal and $\alpha t$ to the right-hand side. For a single cell whose real connections give $\sum w_j x_j = S$ and $\sum w_j = W$, the new optimum is
$$x = \frac{S + \alpha t}{W + \alpha}.$$
With pins at 79 (weight 1) and 29 (weight 2), the plain solution is 45.67; an anchor of weight 4 at 96 moves the cell to $(137 + 384)/7 = 74.43$. The anchor does not force the cell to its target; it balances the target against the cell's connections.

## Where the targets come from

SimPL alternates a lower-bound step and an upper-bound step. The lower bound is the quadratic solve, wirelength-optimal and overlapped. The upper bound is look-ahead legalization: over-full regions are found, expanded until they have enough capacity, and their cells are spread inside them by recursive geometric partitioning that preserves the cells' relative order. The spread positions become the anchor targets for the next solve. As iterations proceed, the anchor weight grows, often linearly with the iteration count, and in SimPL it is also divided by the cell-to-target distance, linearised like a B2B edge, so that the pull behaves like a linear rather than quadratic penalty. The gap between the two bounds shrinks until they meet.

## Choosing the anchor weight

The weight decides how far the cell moves toward its target. Solving $x = p$ for the weight gives $\alpha = (S - pW)/(p - t)$. If the cell should land a fraction $f$ of the way from its plain solution to its target, this simplifies to $\alpha = Wf/(1-f)$, independent of where the pins are: halfway needs $\alpha = W$. Too large a weight early freezes cells at spread positions computed from a poor solution; too small a weight late lets cells collapse back. That schedule is a tunable placer parameter, a Tier 1 change, while the spreading algorithm that produces targets is strategy and the linear solver is core.

## Going deeper

Kim, Lee and Markov, "SimPL: an effective placement algorithm" (ICCAD 2010); Viswanathan, Pan and Chu, "FastPlace 3.0" (ASP-DAC 2007).

label: Force-directed placement
lesson:
# Force-directed placement

Force-directed placement models connections as springs that pull connected cells together and, in its modern forms, density as a force that pushes cells out of crowded regions. It is the physical picture behind quadratic placement and the ancestor of electrostatic placement. The classic algorithm moves one cell at a time to the point where its spring forces balance.

## Springs and the zero-force target

Treat each connection of weight $c_j$ from cell $i$ to cell $j$ as a spring with force $c_j$ times the distance, Hooke's law. The total force on cell $i$ at position $(x_i, y_i)$ is $F_x = \sum_j c_j(x_j - x_i)$ and similarly for y. It vanishes at the weighted centroid of the neighbours:
$$x_i^0 = \frac{\sum_j c_j x_j}{\sum_j c_j}, \qquad y_i^0 = \frac{\sum_j c_j y_j}{\sum_j c_j}.$$
For neighbours at (26, 20) with weight 2 and (10, 39) with weight 1, the zero-force target is (20.67, 26.33). This is exactly the minimiser of the quadratic wirelength for that one cell, which is why force-directed and quadratic placement are two views of the same objective.

## Net force on a cell

At any position the net force tells which way and how hard a cell is pulled. For a cell at (25, 19) with neighbours at x = 17, 26 and 40 and weights 3, 4 and 4, $F_x = 3(17 - 25) + 4(26 - 25) + 4(40 - 25) = -24 + 4 + 60 = 40$, a strong pull to the right. Force magnitude is a natural priority: the iterative algorithm picks the cell with the largest force, or the most connections, and moves it first. Forces also explain why quadratic placement clusters: the springs pull everything toward the centre and nothing pushes back, so modern force-directed placers such as Kraftwerk add a density force computed from the placement's density distribution, which pushes cells from dense to sparse regions.

## The ripple-move algorithm

The classic iterative force-directed algorithm proceeds cell by cell. Pick a cell, compute its zero-force target and round it to the nearest legal grid slot. If the slot is free, move there and lock the cell. If it holds another cell, move in anyway and pick up the displaced cell, which then looks for its own zero-force target, a ripple of moves. If the target is the cell's current location, it stays. Abort conditions stop endless rippling, for example after too many moves without improvement. The rounding step makes this a discrete local search: a cell at (35, 32) with a target that rounds to (17, 38) moves a Manhattan distance of 24. The method is simple and intuitive but slow and greedy, which is why large-scale placers moved to simultaneous analytical methods.

## Going deeper

Quinn and Breuer, "A force directed component placement procedure for printed circuit boards" (IEEE Trans. Circuits and Systems, 1979); Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), section 4.3.3.

label: Bin density and overflow
lesson:
# Bin density and overflow

A global placer controls spreading through density: the cell area in each bin of a grid laid over the placement region, compared with a target. Overflow, the excess area summed over bins, is the number that drives the penalty weight, decides when to stop and predicts how hard legalization will be. Computing it exactly and fast is a core placer kernel.

## Bin density

Divide the region into an $m \times m$ grid of bins. The density of bin $b$ is the area of movable cells overlapping it, divided by its area (or its free area, after subtracting fixed macros and blockages). A cell that straddles bins contributes to each in proportion to its overlap, computed by clipping its rectangle to the bin: a 6 by 2 cell at (4, 11) in a grid of 8 by 8 bins puts 4 by 2 = 8 um$^2$ in the upper-left bin and 2 by 2 = 4 um$^2$ in the upper-right one. During global placement cells may overlap one another, so a bin's density can exceed 1. The bin size is a trade-off: fine bins resolve local crowding, coarse bins are cheaper and smoother.

## Overflow of a bin and of the design

With target density $\rho_t$, the overflow of bin $b$ is $\max(0, A_b^{cells} - \rho_t A_b)$, the area in excess of what the bin may hold. A 12 by 12 bin with 130 um$^2$ of cells at target 0.8 has $130 - 115.2 = 14.8$ um$^2$ of overflow; a bin with 100 um$^2$ has none. The design's total overflow is usually normalised:
$$\tau = \frac{\sum_b \max\left(0, A_b^{cells} - \rho_t A_b\right)}{\sum_i A_i},$$
the fraction of cell area sitting in excess. Electrostatic placers such as RePlAce and OpenROAD's gpl stop global placement when $\tau$ reaches about 0.1 by default.

## Using overflow well

Overflow is an average, so it can hide trouble: a total of 0.08 can come from a few badly over-full bins near a macro, which legalization will resolve only with long moves. Placers therefore also watch the maximum bin density, and routability-driven flows use local targets. Overflow is not differentiable (the max and the clipping create kinks), so nonlinear placers penalise a smoothed density, such as bell-shaped cell potentials (NTUplace) or electrostatic energy (ePlace), and report true overflow only as a stopping metric. Implementation details matter for speed: bin accumulation is a scatter operation over cells, and GPU placers use atomic adds or sorting to accumulate it in parallel.

## Going deeper

Cheng, Kahng, Kang and Wang, "RePlAce: advancing solution quality and routability validation in global placement" (IEEE TCAD, 2019); the OpenROAD documentation for gpl.

label: Smooth wirelength models
lesson:
# Smooth wirelength models

Gradient-based placers need a wirelength that is differentiable, but HPWL is built from max and min, which have kinks wherever two pins tie for an extreme. Smooth wirelength models replace max and min by smooth functions controlled by a parameter $\gamma$. Log-sum-exp, used by APlace, NTUplace and ePlace, was the first widely used choice; weighted-average came later and is more accurate.

## Smoothing the maximum

The function $\gamma \ln \sum_i e^{x_i/\gamma}$ is a smooth approximation of $\max_i x_i$. It is always at least the maximum and at most the maximum plus $\gamma \ln n$, and it approaches the maximum as $\gamma \to 0$. Compute it stably by factoring out the largest value: $\max + \gamma \ln \sum_i e^{(x_i - \max)/\gamma}$, which avoids overflow in the exponentials. For x = 14, 0, 18, 18 and $\gamma$ = 3, the terms are $e^{-4/3}$, $e^{-6}$, 1 and 1, summing to 2.266, so the smooth maximum is $18 + 3\ln 2.266 = 20.454$. Two pins tied at the top push it up by $\gamma \ln 2 = 2.08$; that excess is the price of smoothness.

## Log-sum-exp wirelength

Apply the same idea to the minimum, $\min_i x_i = -\max_i(-x_i)$, and add:
$$W_x^{LSE} = \gamma \ln \sum_i e^{x_i/\gamma} + \gamma \ln \sum_i e^{-x_i/\gamma}.$$
The y part is the same with y coordinates, and the net's estimate is their sum. For pins at x = 10, 18, 13, 1 with $\gamma$ = 4, the smooth maximum is about 19.45 and the smooth negated minimum about -0.37, so $W_x^{LSE} \approx 19.07$ against an exact span of 17. The function is convex, smooth and cheap: each net costs two passes over its pins. Placers sum it over nets with net weights, exactly like HPWL.

## Choosing gamma

Each of the two terms errs by at most $\gamma \ln n$, so LSE overestimates the span by at most $2\gamma \ln n$. A small $\gamma$ gives accuracy but a nearly non-smooth function with large curvature, which forces small optimisation steps; a large $\gamma$ is smooth but inaccurate, and pulls on interior pins that HPWL ignores. Placers therefore tie $\gamma$ to the bin size and shrink it as placement proceeds: ePlace and RePlAce scale it with the density overflow, so it is large when cells are clumped and the exact wirelength matters little, and small near convergence. The x and y coordinates should be in consistent units with $\gamma$, typically bin widths.

## Going deeper

Naylor, Donelly and Sha, US patent 6,301,693 (2001), on log-sum-exp wirelength; Kahng and Wang, "Implementation and extensibility of an analytic placer" (IEEE TCAD, 2005), on APlace.

label: The gradient of log-sum-exp wirelength
lesson:
# The gradient of log-sum-exp wirelength

A nonlinear placer moves each cell along the negative gradient of the objective, so it needs $\partial W/\partial x_i$ for every pin of every net, millions of times per iteration. For log-sum-exp wirelength the gradient is a difference of two softmax weights, a closed form that is cheap, bounded and easy to parallelise.

## Softmax weights

Differentiate $\gamma \ln \sum_j e^{x_j/\gamma}$ with respect to $x_i$: the chain rule gives
$$\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\,\gamma \ln \sum_j e^{x_j/\gamma} = \frac{e^{x_i/\gamma}}{\sum_j e^{x_j/\gamma}},$$
the softmax weight of pin $i$. These weights are positive and sum to 1, and the pins nearest the maximum get most of the weight. For x = 7, 5, 1, 7 with $\gamma$ = 5, the weight of the pin at 5 is $e^{1}/(e^{1.4}\cdot 2 + e^{1} + e^{0.2}) = 0.2256$. Interior pins get small but nonzero weights, unlike HPWL, whose gradient is nonzero only for the extreme pins.

## The full gradient of a net

The minimum term contributes a negative softmax over the negated coordinates, so
$$\frac{\partial W^{LSE}}{\partial x_i} = \frac{e^{x_i/\gamma}}{\sum_j e^{x_j/\gamma}} - \frac{e^{-x_i/\gamma}}{\sum_j e^{-x_j/\gamma}}.$$
Each component lies between -1 and 1. The rightmost pin has a gradient near +1, so descent pulls it left; the leftmost has a gradient near -1 and is pulled right; middle pins feel little. For x = 4, 10, 4 with $\gamma$ = 4, the pin at 4 gets $0.1543 - 0.4498 = -0.2955$. Summed over all pins of a net the gradient is exactly 0, because translating the whole net leaves its length unchanged: a useful unit test for any implementation.

## From pins to cells

A cell's gradient is the sum of the gradients of its pins over all nets it belongs to, each multiplied by the net weight; pin offsets inside the cell do not change the derivative with respect to the cell's position. A cell on two nets with pin gradients 0.12 and 0.15 has total gradient 0.27. Implementations compute the two exponential sums per net in one pass, then each pin's gradient in a second pass, so the cost is linear in the number of pins. On GPUs, one thread per net or per pin works well, with the per-cell sum done by atomic adds or a segmented reduction. The exponentials must be computed after subtracting the net's maximum (and for the other term its minimum) to avoid overflow when $\gamma$ is small.

## Going deeper

Lu et al., "ePlace: electrostatics-based placement using fast Fourier transform and Nesterov's method" (ACM TODAES, 2015); Lin et al., "DREAMPlace" (DAC 2019), on GPU gradient kernels.

label: Weighted-average wirelength
lesson:
# Weighted-average wirelength

The weighted-average (WA) model, proposed by Hsu, Chang and Balabanov, estimates a net's maximum as an exponentially weighted average of its pin coordinates rather than a log-sum. It has a smaller approximation error than log-sum-exp for the same $\gamma$, and it underestimates rather than overestimates. ePlace, RePlAce and DREAMPlace use it by default.

## The weighted-average maximum

Weight every pin by its softmax weight and average the coordinates:
$$\max_i x_i \approx \frac{\sum_i x_i e^{x_i/\gamma}}{\sum_i e^{x_i/\gamma}}.$$
Because it is a weighted average of the coordinates, it can never exceed the true maximum, and it approaches the maximum as $\gamma \to 0$. For x = 17, 14, 5, 7 with $\gamma$ = 4, the weights favour 17 and 14 and the estimate is 15.233, below 17. The minimum is estimated the same way with weights $e^{-x_i/\gamma}$, giving a value at or above the true minimum. Like LSE, it is computed stably by shifting exponents by the maximum (or minimum) first.

## The WA wirelength

The net's x wirelength is the estimated maximum minus the estimated minimum:
$$W_x^{WA} = \frac{\sum_i x_i e^{x_i/\gamma}}{\sum_i e^{x_i/\gamma}} - \frac{\sum_i x_i e^{-x_i/\gamma}}{\sum_i e^{-x_i/\gamma}}.$$
For x = 18, 11, 16 with $\gamma$ = 3, the maximum estimate is about 16.94 and the minimum estimate about 12.26, giving 4.68 against an exact span of 7. The worst-case error of WA is provably smaller than LSE's. Ties show the difference most clearly: when $k$ pins share the maximum, LSE overshoots by about $\gamma \ln k$, while WA averages the tied pins and returns the maximum exactly. The gradient is more complex than for LSE but still closed form, computed from the same per-net sums plus the weighted coordinate sums.

## WA versus LSE in practice

label: Nonlinear placement with a density penalty
lesson:
# Nonlinear placement with a density penalty

Nonlinear analytical placement minimises smooth wirelength plus a weighted density penalty, $W(x) + \lambda D(x)$, by gradient methods, raising $\lambda$ until the cells are spread. APlace, NTUplace3, mPL and the electrostatic placers all follow this penalty method. Its behaviour is set by three things: the gradient step, the schedule of $\lambda$ and the initial balance between the two terms.

## One step on the penalised objective

For fixed $\lambda$, a placer takes gradient-type steps on $f(x) = W(x) + \lambda D(x)$. The gradient on a cell combines the wirelength pull, from the smooth model, and the density push, from the derivative of the smoothed bin densities: $\nabla f = \nabla W + \lambda \nabla D$. With step size $\eta$, plain gradient descent moves a cell to $x - \eta(\partial W/\partial x + \lambda\,\partial D/\partial x)$. A cell at x = 21 with $\partial W/\partial x = -16$, $\partial D/\partial x = -20$, $\lambda = 1$ and $\eta = 0.2$ moves to $21 + 0.2 \cdot 36 = 28.2$: both terms push it right. Real placers use conjugate gradient (NTUplace3) or Nesterov's method (ePlace) rather than plain descent, but the combined gradient is the same.

## Raising the penalty weight

Small $\lambda$ lets wirelength dominate and cells cluster; large $\lambda$ spreads them. The penalty method starts small and raises $\lambda$ over outer iterations, re-solving or continuing the inner optimisation each time, until overflow reaches its target. NTUplace3 doubles $\lambda$ per outer iteration; electrostatic placers multiply it by a factor slightly above 1 every iteration, adjusted by how much wirelength changed. With $\lambda_0 = 0.001$ and factor 1.1, reaching 1 takes $\lceil \ln 1000/\ln 1.1 \rceil = 73$ iterations. Raising $\lambda$ too fast freezes a poor arrangement; too slowly wastes runtime with cells hardly moving.

## Balancing the two forces at the start

The initial $\lambda$ should make the wirelength and density forces comparable, otherwise one term is ignored. A standard initialisation is the ratio of gradient norms, $\lambda_0 = \|\nabla W\|_1/\|\nabla D\|_1$, computed at the initial placement. If the wirelength gradients of four cells are 26, -26, -8, 21 (norm 81) and the density gradients are -263, 120, -76, 241 (norm 700), then $\lambda_0 = 0.1157$. The initial placement itself matters: placers often start from a quadratic solution so that the nonlinear phase begins with sensible relative positions. All of these numbers, the initial weight rule, the growth factor and the overflow target, are parameters an agent can tune without touching the solver.

## Going deeper

label: Electrostatics-based placement
prereqs: Nonlinear placement with a density penalty
lesson:
# Electrostatics-based placement

Electrostatics-based placement, introduced by ePlace and extended by RePlAce and DREAMPlace, models every cell as a positive charge equal to its area. Density overflow becomes electric potential energy, and the density gradient becomes the electric force that pushes charges apart. The analogy gives a global, smooth density penalty that handles standard cells and macros together.

## Cells as charges, density as energy

Each cell $i$ is a charge $q_i$ equal to its area, spread over its footprint. The charge density over the region defines a potential $\psi$ through Poisson's equation, $\nabla^2\psi = -\rho$, and the density penalty is the system's potential energy:
$$N(x) = \frac{1}{2}\sum_i q_i \psi_i.$$
For charges 4, 1 and 6 at potentials 5.6, 3.6 and 0.5, $N = (22.4 + 3.6 + 3)/2 = 14.5$. Energy is high when charge is concentrated, because nearby charges raise each other's potential, and low when it is spread evenly, so minimising $W + \lambda N$ trades wirelength against uniform spreading. To make the even distribution the minimum, the density's mean is subtracted (a neutral system).

## Density force as electric force

The gradient of the energy with respect to a cell's position is its charge times the electric field, $\nabla_i N = -q_i E_i$ with $E = -\nabla\psi$. So the density force on a cell is $q_i E_i$, pointing from dense regions to sparse ones. A cell of area 5 in a field $E = (1.5, 0.7)$ feels a force of magnitude $5\sqrt{1.5^2 + 0.7^2} = 8.276$. Larger cells, such as macros, feel proportionally larger forces, so mixed-size placement needs no special treatment, though a preconditioner that divides each cell's gradient by its pin count plus $\lambda$ times its charge keeps steps balanced across sizes. The field is computed once per iteration for the whole grid, then sampled at every cell.

## Fillers and the overflow target

If the cells cover less area than the target density allows, the electrostatic force would keep spreading them across all the whitespace, lengthening wires. ePlace inserts filler cells, charges with no connections, so that movable plus filler area equals the target density times the free area. With 24100 um$^2$ of free area, target 0.7 and 9640 um$^2$ of movable cells, the fillers need $16870 - 9640 = 7230$ um$^2$, which is 1446 fillers of 5 um$^2$. Fillers move freely and occupy whitespace, so real cells stop spreading once the density is uniform at target. They are removed before legalization. The placer stops when the overflow of real cells reaches its target, about 0.1.

## Going deeper

label: Solving the density Poisson equation by FFT
lesson:
# Solving the density Poisson equation by FFT

Electrostatic placement solves Poisson's equation for the potential on the bin grid at every iteration. A spectral method does it in $O(m^2 \log m)$ time for an $m \times m$ grid: expand the density in cosine modes, divide each mode by its Laplacian eigenvalue and transform back. This step is why the method scales, and it is the kernel GPU placers accelerate with fast cosine transforms.

## Cosine modes diagonalise the Laplacian

On a rectangular grid with zero-flux (Neumann) boundaries, the density can be expanded in cosine modes $\cos(\omega_u x)\cos(\omega_v y)$, with $\omega_u = \pi u/m$ for unit bins on an $m$-bin grid. Each mode is an eigenfunction of the Laplacian: $\nabla^2[\cos(\omega_u x)\cos(\omega_v y)] = -(\omega_u^2 + \omega_v^2)\cos(\omega_u x)\cos(\omega_v y)$. So if the density has coefficient $a_{uv}$ for a mode, the potential solving $\nabla^2\psi = -\rho$ has coefficient $a_{uv}/(\omega_u^2 + \omega_v^2)$. With m = 16, u = 6, v = 3 and $a = 0.3$, $\omega_u = 1.1781$ and $\omega_v = 0.5890$, so the potential coefficient is $0.3/1.7349 = 0.1729$. The constant mode $u = v = 0$ is dropped, which is the neutrality condition.

## The field from the same coefficients

The field $E = -\nabla\psi$ follows by differentiating the modes, so it too is a sum of sine-cosine products with the same coefficients:
$$E_x = \sum_{u,v} \frac{a_{uv}\,\omega_u}{\omega_u^2 + \omega_v^2}\sin(\omega_u x)\cos(\omega_v y),$$
and similarly for $E_y$ with the roles swapped. Each field component is one inverse transform of a mixed sine and cosine type. Low-frequency modes, with small $\omega$, get the largest amplification: they describe large-scale imbalance, such as all cells on the left half, and produce long-range forces, while high-frequency modes describe local clumps and produce short-range ones. That built-in multiscale behaviour is a large part of why electrostatic spreading works well.

## Why the FFT makes it scale

A direct transform computes $m^2$ coefficients, each a sum over $m^2$ bins: $m^4$ operations. A fast cosine transform does the same work in about $m^2 \log_2(m^2)$ operations, a ratio of $m^2/(2\log_2 m)$, which for $m = 512$ is about 14564. One placement iteration needs a forward transform for the coefficients and inverse transforms for the potential and the two field components, all on the bin grid, independent of the number of cells. Bin counts are usually powers of two near the square root of the cell count. Accumulating the density onto the grid and sampling the field at cells are scatter and gather operations; on GPUs, DREAMPlace implements the cosine transforms via FFT routines.

## Going deeper

Lu et al., "ePlace" (ACM TODAES, 2015), section on the spectral Poisson solver; Lin et al., "DREAMPlace" (DAC 2019), on DCT-based density computation.

label: Nesterov's method with Lipschitz step estimates
lesson:
# Nesterov's method with Lipschitz step estimates

ePlace solves the penalised placement problem with Nesterov's accelerated gradient method, whose momentum gives faster convergence than plain gradient descent on smooth problems. Because the Lipschitz constant of the placement objective is unknown and changes as $\lambda$ grows, ePlace predicts the step length from the last two iterates. This combination is the optimiser inside RePlAce, OpenROAD's gpl and DREAMPlace.

## Step length from a local Lipschitz estimate

For a function with $L$-Lipschitz gradient, a safe gradient step is $1/L$. ePlace estimates $L$ from the latest two points:
$$\alpha_k = \frac{\|v_k - v_{k-1}\|}{\|\nabla f(v_k) - \nabla f(v_{k-1})\|}.$$
If the position moved by (4, 6), norm 7.2111, and the gradient changed by (-2, 11), norm 11.1803, then $\alpha_k = 0.645$. This is a secant estimate of the inverse curvature, related to Barzilai-Borwein steps. ePlace adds backtracking: if the step computed after moving predicts a much smaller step than the one used, the step is recomputed, so a bad estimate does not destabilise the run. Vectors here are all cell coordinates stacked, so the norms are over millions of entries.

## The momentum sequence

Nesterov's method maintains a scalar sequence $a_0 = 1$, $a_{k+1} = (1 + \sqrt{4a_k^2 + 1})/2$, giving 1, 1.618, 2.194, 2.750, 3.295 and so on, growing roughly like $k/2$. The momentum coefficient is $(a_k - 1)/a_{k+1}$: 0 at the first step, 0.2817 at the second, and approaching 1 later. From $a_k = 3.2949$, $a_{k+1} = 3.8326$ and the coefficient is 0.5988. Increasing momentum is what accelerates convergence on smooth convex problems from $O(1/k)$ to $O(1/k^2)$. Placement is not convex, but the acceleration still helps, and the schedule can be restarted if the objective rises. The sequence depends only on the iteration count, not on the problem, so it costs nothing to compute; what makes the method work is pairing it with a good step length at every iteration.

## One full Nesterov update

Each iteration takes a gradient step from the look-ahead point and then extrapolates:
$$u_{k+1} = v_k - \alpha_k\nabla f(v_k), \qquad v_{k+1} = u_{k+1} + \frac{a_k - 1}{a_{k+1}}(u_{k+1} - u_k).$$
For one coordinate with $u_k = 75$, $v_k = 70$, gradient 6, $\alpha = 0.1$ and $a_k = 2.7486$: $u_{k+1} = 69.4$, $a_{k+1} = 3.2937$, the coefficient is 0.5309 and $v_{k+1} = 69.4 + 0.5307(69.4 - 75) = 66.427$. The gradient is evaluated at the extrapolated point $v$, not at $u$. Note the order of work: the step is taken from the look-ahead point, and the momentum term then reuses the difference between the new and old gradient-step points, so the method stores two position vectors rather than one. Per iteration the cost is one wirelength gradient, one density solve and a few vector operations, all parallel across cells.

Nesterov, "A method of solving a convex programming problem with convergence rate O(1/k^2)" (Soviet Math. Doklady, 1983); Lu et al., "ePlace" (ACM TODAES, 2015), section on Nesterov's method with Lipschitz prediction.

lesson:
# DREAMPlace and GPU-accelerated placement

DREAMPlace recast electrostatics-based global placement as training a neural network: cell positions are the trainable parameters, wirelength plus density is the loss, and a deep-learning toolkit (PyTorch) provides the optimisation loop and GPU execution. With custom GPU operators it ran global placement more than an order of magnitude faster than CPU implementations with similar quality, and it became a platform for placement research.

## Placement as training

In DREAMPlace, the x and y coordinates of movable cells form a parameter tensor. The forward pass computes weighted-average wirelength and electrostatic density energy; the backward pass computes their gradients; an optimiser such as Nesterov's method updates the parameters. The algorithm is ePlace's, with the same smooth wirelength, spectral density solve, penalty schedule and fillers, so quality is similar to RePlAce; what changes is the execution. Expressing placement in a deep-learning framework brings automatic differentiation for new cost terms, GPU memory management, and easy experimentation, at the price of depending on the framework's runtime.

## Custom operators and GPU kernels

A naive implementation using generic tensor operations would be slow and memory-hungry, because wirelength is a sum over irregular nets. DREAMPlace writes key operators by hand, with forward and backward CUDA kernels: wirelength over nets and pins, density accumulation onto bins, and the Poisson solve through fast cosine transforms. Net-level and bin-level parallelism map well to thousands of GPU threads. Scatter operations, adding cell contributions into bins or pin gradients into cells, use atomic additions, and since floating-point addition is not associative, their nondeterministic order can make two runs differ slightly unless deterministic reductions are used. Later versions also moved legalization and detailed placement onto the GPU, since those became the bottleneck once global placement was fast.

## What it changed for tool designers

DREAMPlace showed that a placer can be built from differentiable operators, so a new objective (a routability term, a timing term, a new density model) is added by writing one operator with a gradient, without rewriting the optimiser. Speed changes how placement is used: when global placement takes a minute instead of half an hour, an agent or a design-space exploration loop can try many parameter settings and floorplans. End-to-end speedup is limited by the stages not accelerated, Amdahl's law in practice. Its results also illustrate that implementation details, such as precision, kernel approximations and stopping rules, shift QoR slightly, so comparisons between placers must use the same metrics, legalizer and detailed placer.

## Going deeper

Lin, Dhar, Li, Ren, Khailany and Pan, "DREAMPlace: deep learning toolkit-enabled GPU acceleration for modern VLSI placement" (DAC 2019; IEEE TCAD 2021); the DREAMPlace open-source repository documentation.

# Legalization and displacement

Legalization takes the overlapping, off-grid output of global placement and produces a legal placement: every cell in a row, on a site, without overlap. It should change the global solution as little as possible, so its quality is measured by displacement, how far cells moved. Total, maximum and squared displacement each capture a different risk to wirelength and timing.

## What legalization must achieve

A legal placement puts every standard cell with its bottom edge on a row, its left edge on a site boundary, in the row's orientation, with no overlap with other cells, macros or blockages, and inside any region constraint. Global placement guarantees none of this. Legalization finds the nearest legal arrangement: it assigns each cell a row and an x position. Because the global placer worked hard to minimise wirelength, the legalizer's objective is to preserve its solution, which it measures as displacement between the global position $(x_i, y_i)$ and the legal position $(x_i', y_i')$. Cells keep their relative order where possible, since reordering lengthens wires unpredictably.

## Measuring displacement

The displacement of a cell is usually the Manhattan distance $|x_i - x_i'| + |y_i - y_i'|$. Total displacement sums it over cells; maximum displacement reports the worst single move; average displacement is the total over the cell count. For moves of 5, 6 and 6 um, the total is 17 um and the maximum 6 um. Some legalizers minimise the sum of squared displacements, $\sum_i (x_i - x_i')^2$ (Abacus does, within a row): squaring penalises a single long move more than several short ones, which tends to keep the maximum small. For moves of 6, 1 and 2 um the squared sum is $36 + 1 + 4 = 41$.

## Why the metric matters downstream

Total displacement correlates with the wirelength lost in legalization, but timing is sensitive to individual moves: one critical cell moved 80 rows can break a path even when the total is small. Large maximum displacement often signals that global placement left a local overflow, for example near a macro edge, that legalization had to resolve by pushing cells far away. Good flows therefore report both metrics, bound the maximum, weight timing-critical cells more heavily, and feed hot spots back to global placement rather than accept long moves. Legalization is also run repeatedly during optimisation, after buffering and sizing, so its speed and incremental behaviour matter as much as its quality.

## Going deeper

lesson:
# Tetris legalization

Tetris legalization is the simplest practical legalizer: sort cells by x and drop each into the row where it moves least, at the leftmost free position. It runs in $O(n \log n)$ for sorting plus a cheap scan per cell, and it is the baseline every better legalizer is measured against. Its greedy order explains both its speed and its typical failure.

## Sort, then place greedily

Sort the cells by their global x coordinate. Keep, for each row, the right edge of the cells already placed in it, initially the row's left boundary. For each cell in sorted order, consider every row (or the rows near the cell): the cell would go at $x = \max(x_{desired}, \text{right edge of that row})$ and its displacement would be $|x - x_{desired}| + |y_{row} - y_{desired}|$. Put it in the row with the smallest displacement, ties broken by a fixed rule, and advance that row's right edge by the cell's width. In a single row with cells wanting x = 2, 6, 10 and 19 and widths 6, 4, 2 and 5, the cells land at 2, 8, 12 and 19.

## Choosing the row

The row choice trades vertical against horizontal movement. A cell that wants (1, 2) with rows at y = 0 and y = 2 may prefer the upper row even though another row is emptier, because vertical moves cost displacement too. With two rows and many cells, a cell late in the order often finds its preferred row filled up to the right of its desired x, so it either shifts right in that row or moves to a neighbouring row. Restricting the search to a few rows above and below keeps each step cheap; scanning every row is $O(n \cdot \text{rows})$. Implementations track free segments per row so that macros and blockages, which split rows, are handled by the same scan.

## Strengths and failure modes

Tetris is fast, simple and always legal if there is room. Its weakness is the greedy order: early cells never move to make room for later ones, so cells at the right end of crowded rows can be pushed far right or into distant rows, giving a long tail of displacement. It also ignores the original relative order across rows and minimises only each cell's own displacement. Total displacement in a two-row example might be small while one late cell moves several units. Improvements include processing from both ends, limiting per-row fill, and replacing the greedy choice with Abacus-style clustering, which lets earlier cells shift left to share the displacement. Tetris remains useful as a quick legalizer inside fast loops.

label: Legalization with Abacus
lesson:
# Legalization with Abacus

Abacus improves on Tetris by letting cells already placed in a row shift to make room, choosing positions that minimise total squared displacement in that row. It does this with clusters: groups of abutting cells that move together to their collective optimum. Abacus became a standard legalizer because it is nearly as fast as Tetris and much better in quality.

## Clusters and their optimal position

Within one row, keep the cells in their x order and require no overlap. If cells $1..k$ abut as a cluster starting at $x_c$, cell $i$ sits at $x_c + o_i$, where $o_i$ is the total width of the cells before it in the cluster. Minimising $\sum_i e_i(x_c + o_i - x_i')^2$, with $e_i$ a weight such as cell area or 1, gives
$$x_c = \frac{\sum_i e_i (x_i' - o_i)}{\sum_i e_i},$$
then clamped to the row boundaries. Two cells wanting 23 and 26 with the first 7 wide form a cluster at $(23 + (26 - 7))/2 = 21$: the first cell moves left by 2 and the second right by 2. Abacus stores per cluster $e_c = \sum e_i$, $q_c = \sum e_i(x_i' - o_i)$ and total width $w_c$, so $x_c = q_c/e_c$.

## Adding cells and merging clusters

Cells are processed in x order. A cell that starts at or after the right end of the last cluster begins a new cluster at its desired position. Otherwise it joins the last cluster: $e_c \mathrel{+}= e_i$, $q_c \mathrel{+}= e_i(x_i' - w_c)$, $w_c \mathrel{+}= w_i$. The cluster then moves to $q_c/e_c$, clamped. If it now overlaps its left neighbour, the two merge: the left cluster absorbs the right one with $q \mathrel{+}= q_c - e_c w_{left}$, and the merged cluster is re-collapsed, possibly cascading left. Each merge reduces the number of clusters, so the total work in a row is linear in its cells. In a row with cells c3 and c4 overlapping near x = 23, they cluster at x = 22, and c4 ends at 26.

## Choosing rows and the full algorithm

The full Abacus algorithm processes cells globally in x order. For each cell it tries rows near its desired y, trial-places it at the end of each candidate row with the clustering procedure, computes the cost (the change in squared displacement, including the vertical move), and commits the cell to the cheapest row. Trial placements do not modify the row permanently, and the search stops early when the vertical distance alone exceeds the best cost found. Abacus legalizes in continuous x and then snaps clusters to the site grid. Weighting cells by area keeps large cells from moving much. Its limits are multi-row-height cells and complex rules such as edge spacing, which need extensions; modern legalizers built on it handle those with additional constraints.

## Going deeper

label: Legality rules: sites, rails and regions
lesson:
# Legality rules: sites, rails and regions

At advanced nodes, legal means much more than "in a row and not overlapping". Power rail alignment, multi-row cells, fence and guide regions, blockages and neighbour-dependent spacing all constrain where cells may go. These rules live in the placer's core: every downstream engine assumes their output holds, so a legalizer that misses one corrupts the whole flow.

## Rows, sites and rail alignment

A cell must start on a site boundary of a row and use that row's orientation. Rows alternate N and FS so that adjacent rows share rails, so a cell moved between rows of different parity must be flipped. Multi-row-height cells, such as double-height flip-flops, span two rows and can only start in rows where their bottom rail matches: a double-height cell expecting VSS at the bottom cannot start in a row whose bottom rail is VDD. Some libraries add well or implant rules that force spacing between cells of different types, and tap cells must be present at regular intervals. All of these are discrete constraints on the slot assignment, checked exactly.

## Regions and blockages

A fence region is exclusive: its member cells must be placed inside it and no other cells may enter. A guide region only attracts its members, without excluding others. Hard placement blockages forbid all cells, for example under a sensitive analog block; partial blockages cap the allowed density, leaving room for routing. FIXED instances in DEF, such as macros and pre-placed cells, occupy their sites permanently. A legalizer represents all of these by splitting rows into usable segments per region, so a row becomes a set of intervals, each with an owner. Global placement must also see them, otherwise it spreads fenced cells outside their fence and legalization moves them far.

## Neighbour rules and why legality is core

Some rules depend on the neighbour: edge-type spacing requires a gap between particular cell edges, and pin-access rules can make two specific cells unroutable when abutted. These make legality a property of pairs of adjacent cells, not just of each cell's slot, so the legalizer must check the left and right neighbours whenever it places a cell. Because rules like these grow with each technology, a placer is designed with legality as a small, heavily tested core: a slot model and a rule checker that every move must pass. Heuristics that choose positions can change freely, but the guarantee cannot. A plug-in that prefers some arrangement may score it, but only the core decides what is legal.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter 4; the ISPD 2015 and ICCAD 2017 placement contest descriptions, on fence regions and advanced-node rules.

label: Detailed placement by cell swapping
prereqs: Incremental HPWL after a cell move
lesson:
# Detailed placement by cell swapping

Detailed placement improves a legal placement with local moves that keep it legal. The simplest move swaps two cells of equal width; more general moves shift, reorder or reassign cells. Each move is accepted only if it lowers the cost, evaluated incrementally on the nets that touch the moved cells. Swaps are the building block of every detailed placer.

## Evaluating a swap

Swapping cells a and b exchanges their positions. If they have equal widths, the result is automatically legal. Only nets touching a or b change, so
$$\Delta W = \sum_{e \ni a \text{ or } b} \left(\mathrm{HPWL}_e^{after} - \mathrm{HPWL}_e^{before}\right).$$
With a at (8, 25) and b at (14, 7), a on one net with pins at (12, 14) and (3, 14), b on two nets, the deltas might be -2 for a's net and $+3$ and -11 for b's nets, a total of -10: the swap shortens wiring by 10 um and is accepted. A swap with $\Delta W \ge 0$ is rejected in a greedy detailed placer. Unequal widths make a swap need extra shifting of neighbours, which is why many swap moves are restricted to same-width cells or to cells with enough whitespace nearby.

## Shared nets and double counting

A net that contains both a and b must be evaluated with both cells moved at the same time. If the net's other pins are fixed, swapping a and b exchanges two of its pin positions and leaves the set of positions, and therefore the HPWL, unchanged. Evaluating the swap as "move a, then move b" with the other cell still in its old place would get this net wrong. Implementations collect the union of nets of both cells, deduplicate it, and recompute each once with both new positions. The same care applies to cells with two pins on one net, where the net appears twice in the cell's net list.

## Global swap and search strategy

Trying all pairs is quadratic, so detailed placers choose candidates smartly. Global swap, as in FastDP, computes for each cell its optimal region, the area where its nets would be shortest, and tries to swap it with a cell or a gap in that region. Vertical swap tries cells in the rows just above and below. The placer sweeps over all cells, accepts improving moves, and repeats passes until the gain per pass falls below a threshold. Because each move is evaluated incrementally in time proportional to the pins involved, a pass over a million cells takes seconds. Timing-driven variants add the change in slack or in weighted wirelength to the cost.

## Going deeper

Pan, Viswanathan and Chu, "An efficient and effective detailed placement algorithm" (ICCAD 2005), on FastDP; Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), section 4.4.

label: The optimal region of a cell
lesson:
# The optimal region of a cell

For a single cell with every other cell fixed, the positions that minimise the total HPWL of its nets form a rectangle, its optimal region, found from medians of the other pins' bounds. Detailed placers use it to decide where a cell wants to go before they search for a legal spot there, and the computation is a neat application of the median minimising a sum of distances.

## Why medians appear

Remove cell c and look at each of its nets: the remaining pins span an interval $[l_j, r_j]$ in x. With c at x, the net's x span is $(r_j - l_j) + \mathrm{dist}(x, [l_j, r_j])$, so the cell's total cost is a constant plus $\sum_j \mathrm{dist}(x, [l_j, r_j])$. This is a convex piecewise-linear function of x whose slope is the number of interval endpoints below x minus the number of nets, so it is minimised wherever exactly half of the $2k$ endpoints lie below x. Sort the $2k$ endpoints; any x between the $k$-th and the $(k+1)$-th is optimal. For two nets with others' intervals [11, 11] and [6, 46], the sorted bounds are 6, 11, 11, 46 and the optimal x is exactly 11.

## The gain from moving there

Comparing the cost at the current position with the cost in the optimal interval tells how much the cell could gain. For nets with others' intervals [9, 44] and [24, 51], the sorted bounds are 9, 24, 44, 51, so the optimal interval is [24, 44]. With the cell at x = 60, the spans are 51 and 36, total 87; anywhere in [24, 44] they are 35 and 27, total 62, a potential gain of 25. The y dimension is computed independently, so the optimal region is a rectangle, $[x_k, x_{k+1}] \times [y_k, y_{k+1}]$. The Manhattan distance from the cell to that rectangle measures how misplaced the cell is.

## Using optimal regions in detailed placement

FastDP's global swap uses the optimal region as a target: for a cell, find the optimal region, then try swapping with each cell in it or moving into a gap there, and accept the best improving move, which must account for the moved partner's own change in cost. The region ignores legality and other cells' preferences, so it is a guide, not a destination. Because every cell's region depends on the others, the computation is repeated as cells move. Cells whose region contains their current position are already locally optimal and can be skipped, which prunes most of the work in later passes. Timing-driven versions weight the intervals by net criticality, which turns medians into weighted medians.

## Going deeper

Pan, Viswanathan and Chu, "An efficient and effective detailed placement algorithm" (ICCAD 2005); Goto, "An efficient algorithm for the two-dimensional placement problem in electrical circuit layout" (IEEE Trans. Circuits and Systems, 1981).

problems.q: Cell c is on 3 nets: net n1's other pins are at x = 40; net n2's other pins are at x = 9, 47, 8; net n3's other pins are at x = 53. Ignoring c, each net's other pins span an x interval. label: Sliding-window reordering
lesson:
# Sliding-window reordering

Local reordering takes a small window of consecutive cells in a row, tries every order of them packed into the same span and keeps the best. With three or four cells the enumeration is tiny, and sliding the window along every row catches improvements that pairwise swaps miss. It is a standard pass in FastDP-style and GPU detailed placers.

## Packing a window in a new order

Take $k$ adjacent cells in a row occupying a span from $x_0$. For an order $\pi$, pack the cells left to right from $x_0$ with no gaps (or preserving the window's total whitespace in fixed positions): the first cell sits at $x_0$, the next at $x_0$ plus the first width, and so on. Pin positions follow from cell positions; for a pin at a cell's centre it is $x + w/2$. With widths A = 2, B = 4 and C = 8 packed from 18 in order A B C, the centres are 19, 22 and 30. The packing stays legal because the cells fill exactly the same span, so only wirelength changes, and only on nets that touch the window.

## Trying every order

With $k$ cells there are $k!$ orders: 6 for three cells, 24 for four, 120 for five. For each order, compute the x span of every net touching the window and sum. The y spans do not change, because the cells stay in the row. Keep the order with the smallest sum, and apply it if it beats the current order. Example: A to fixed pins at 28 and 55, B to 39, C to 13, and a net from B to C, with widths 4, 2, 8 from x = 15. The current order costs some total; trying all six orders finds that C B A costs only 54 um. Nets between two window cells must be evaluated with both cells' new positions.

## Window size and sweeping

The window slides across each row with some overlap, for example by one or two cells at a time, so an improvement found in one window can enable another in the next. Window size is a trade-off: $k!$ grows fast, so $k = 3$ or 4 is typical, and dynamic programming over positions can handle somewhat larger windows when cells must stay in their row segment. Because windows in different rows, or far apart in one row, do not share cells, many can be optimised in parallel if they also share no nets, which is how GPU detailed placers batch them. The pass is cheap and complements swaps, which change positions of distant cells, and independent-set matching, which reassigns several cells at once.

## Going deeper

Pan, Viswanathan and Chu, "An efficient and effective detailed placement algorithm" (ICCAD 2005); Lin et al., "ABCDPlace: accelerated batch-based concurrent detailed placement on multithreaded CPUs and GPUs" (IEEE TCAD, 2020).

label: Independent-set matching
lesson:
# Independent-set matching

Independent-set matching picks a set of same-size cells that share no nets, so their wirelength costs are independent of each other, and reassigns them among their own locations by solving a minimum-cost bipartite matching. One matching can move many cells at once to a jointly optimal arrangement, which pairwise swaps cannot find.

## Why the cells must be independent

If two chosen cells share a net, the cost of putting one in a slot depends on where the other goes, and the assignment cost no longer decomposes into a sum of independent terms. Choosing cells that share no net, an independent set in the graph where cells are adjacent if they share a net, makes each cell's cost depend only on its own slot. Then the cost of putting cell $i$ in slot $j$ is just the HPWL of $i$'s nets with $i$ at $j$, computed once per pair. Cells are also chosen with the same width (and height), so any assignment of cells to the set's locations is legal. In practice the set is drawn from a local window, so the slots are near each other.

## Solving the matching

With $n$ cells and their $n$ current locations as slots, build an $n \times n$ cost matrix $c_{ij}$ and find the permutation minimising $\sum_i c_{i\pi(i)}$, the linear assignment problem. The Hungarian algorithm solves it in $O(n^3)$; for $n = 3$ there are just six permutations. For three cells A, B and C, the identity assignment might cost 237 um and the best permutation, sending A to B's spot, B to C's and C to A's, 194 um, a gain of 43 um. Because the costs are exact HPWL of independent nets, the gain predicted by the matching is exactly the gain realised.

## ISM in a detailed placer

A detailed placer runs ISM repeatedly: pick a seed cell, grow an independent set of similar cells in a window around it, typically up to a few dozen cells, solve the matching, apply it, and continue. Larger sets find better arrangements but cost more per solve and are harder to keep independent. ISM is used in NTUplace3's detailed placer and in GPU detailed placers such as ABCDPlace, where many independent sets are solved concurrently, since sets that share no nets can be processed in parallel. Combined with global swap and local reordering, it forms the core move set of modern wirelength-driven detailed placement.

## Going deeper

Chen et al., "NTUplace3: an analytical placer for large-scale mixed-size designs" (IEEE TCAD, 2008); Lin et al., "ABCDPlace" (IEEE TCAD, 2020).

label: Net delay as a function of placement
prereqs: Elmore delay of an RC tree
lesson:
# Net delay as a function of placement

Placement fixes the length of every wire before any wire exists, and wire length sets wire delay. Estimating a net's delay from its placement, with HPWL or a tree length feeding the Elmore model, is how a timing-driven placer sees the consequences of its moves. The key fact is that distributed wire delay grows with the square of length.

## Wire delay from placed pins

For a two-pin net, the routed length is estimated by the Manhattan distance between the pins, which equals its HPWL and its Steiner tree. With resistance $r$ and capacitance $c$ per unit length, a uniform RC line of length $L$ has Elmore delay $rcL^2/2$, half the value of a lumped model, because each bit of resistance charges only the capacitance beyond it. A driver at (0, 370) and a sink at (860, 860) give $L = 1350$ um; with $r = 0.5$ ohm/um and $c = 0.15$ fF/um the wire delay is $0.5 \cdot 0.15 \cdot 1350^2/2 = 68344$ ohm-fF, 68.34 ps. For multi-pin nets a Steiner or spanning tree from the placement gives the topology, and the Elmore delay to each sink follows from the tree.

## Adding the driver and the load

The full stage delay includes the driver's output resistance $R_d$ charging the whole wire and the sink pin capacitance $C_L$:
$$D = R_d(cL + C_L) + rL\left(\frac{cL}{2} + C_L\right).$$
The first term is linear in $L$, the second has a quadratic part. For $L = 580$ um, $r = 1$ ohm/um, $c = 0.15$ fF/um, $R_d = 700$ ohm and $C_L = 7$ fF: the driver term is $700 \cdot 94 = 65800$ ohm-fF and the wire term $580 \cdot 50.5 = 29290$ ohm-fF, 95.09 ps in total. Short nets are dominated by the driver term, so cell sizing matters more than placement for them; long nets are dominated by the wire term, where placement matters most.

## What this means for a placer

Because wire delay scales with $L^2$, stretching a net by a factor of 2.5, for example when a congestion-driven move pushes a sink away, multiplies its wire delay by 6.25. A placer that trades a little wirelength on critical nets for a lot of wirelength elsewhere can therefore improve timing even while total HPWL rises. The quadratic law also explains why very long nets are not fixed by placement at all but by buffering, which breaks them into segments whose delays add linearly. Timing-driven placers run a fast timer on these estimates: wire parasitics from placement, cell delays from Liberty, and the timing graph from STA, refreshed every few iterations.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter 8 on timing closure; Rabaey, Chandrakasan and Nikolic, "Digital Integrated Circuits" (2nd ed., 2003), chapter 4 on wires.

label: Timing-driven placement
prereqs: Net delay as a function of placement
lesson:
# Timing-driven placement

A wirelength-driven placer treats all nets alike, so critical paths end up no shorter than any other. Timing-driven placement fixes this by weighting nets according to their timing criticality, computed from static timing analysis on the current placement. Net weighting is simple, works with every placement algorithm, and is what OpenROAD's gpl and RePlAce use in timing-driven mode.

## Criticality and net weights

After a timing run, each net gets its worst slack $s$, the minimum slack over paths through it. A criticality maps slack to [0, 1]: one common form is $c = \min(1, \max(0, -s/|WNS|))$, which is 0 for nets with non-negative slack and 1 for nets on the worst path. The net weight is then $w = 1 + \alpha c^\beta$, with $\alpha$ setting the maximum boost and $\beta$ concentrating it on the most critical nets. With WNS = -125 ps, $\alpha = 2$ and $\beta = 3$, a net with slack -55 ps has $c = 0.44$ and $w = 1 + 2 \cdot 0.44^3 = 1.1704$. Many variants exist; the shape matters less than updating the weights as timing changes.

## Weighted wirelength and its effect

The placer then minimises $\sum_e w_e \mathrm{WL}_e$. In quadratic placement, a heavier spring pulls harder: a movable cell between a fixed pin at x = 3 on a critical net and a fixed pin at x = 74 on a non-critical net sits at the midpoint 38.5 when weights are equal, and at $(1.5625 \cdot 3 + 74)/2.5625 = 30.71$ when the critical net weighs 1.5625, a shift of 7.79 um toward the critical pin. In nonlinear placement the weighted gradient does the same. The effect is to shorten critical nets at the expense of non-critical ones, ideally without much change in total wirelength, since most nets have slack to spare.

## Keeping weights current

Criticalities change as the placement changes, so timing-driven placers re-run timing periodically, for example at fixed overflow milestones, and update weights, often blending new with old weights to avoid oscillation: a net heavily weighted becomes short, gains slack, loses weight and drifts long again. Early in global placement, wire estimates are poor and timing is not yet meaningful, so the first updates come after cells have spread. Path-based methods, which constrain the delay of specific critical paths directly, are more precise but harder to scale; net weighting is the robust default. The weighting function, its parameters and the update schedule are change-surface parameters, while the timer it calls is a separate engine behind an interface.

## Going deeper

label: Routability-driven placement
lesson:
# Routability-driven placement

A placement with short wires can still be unroutable if too many wires must pass through one region. Routability-driven placement estimates routing demand during placement and spreads cells out of congested regions. RUDY, Spindler and Johannes's rectangular uniform wire density, is the cheapest widely used estimate: it needs only net bounding boxes, no routing.

## RUDY wire density

RUDY assumes each net's wire is spread uniformly over its bounding box. A net with box $w \times h$ has estimated wirelength $w + h$, its HPWL, so its wire density inside the box is
$$d = \frac{w + h}{wh},$$
in units of wire length per unit area. A net spanning 21 by 5 um has density $26/105 = 0.2476$ um per um$^2$. Small boxes have high density: a local net with pins close together concentrates its wire in a small area, which is exactly the kind of local crowding that creates routing hot spots. Degenerate boxes with zero width or height are clamped to a minimum size, typically one bin or one track pitch, so the density stays finite.

## Demand per bin

The routing demand in a bin is the sum over nets of their density times the area of their box inside the bin:
$$D_b = \sum_e d_e\, |B_e \cap b|.$$
For a 10 by 10 bin overlapped 70 um$^2$ by a net of density 0.2054 and not at all by another, the demand is 14.38 um of wire. Summed over all bins, each net contributes exactly its HPWL, so RUDY redistributes wirelength rather than inventing it. The computation is a rectangle-overlap scatter over nets and bins, linear in the total number of net-bin overlaps, and on GPUs it uses the same accumulation tricks as the density map.

## From demand to congestion and action

Capacity is the wire length the bin can carry: with $L$ usable layers at track pitch $p$, a $B \times B$ bin offers roughly $L B^2/p$ um of wire, less what power stripes and blockages take. The congestion ratio is demand over capacity, and bins above 1 are predicted to overflow. RUDY ignores detours, pin access and layer direction, so it is a fast proxy; RePlAce and OpenROAD can instead call a global router for a more accurate congestion map at milestones. Placers act on the map by inflating cells in congested bins, lowering the local target density, or adding the congestion as a penalty, so cells spread where wires crowd.

## Going deeper

Spindler and Johannes, "Fast and accurate routing demand estimation for efficient routability-driven placement" (DATE 2007); Cheng, Kahng, Kang and Wang, "RePlAce" (IEEE TCAD, 2019), on routability mode.

label: Cell inflation for congestion
lesson:
# Cell inflation for congestion

Cell inflation is the simplest way to make a density-driven placer care about congestion: temporarily enlarge the cells that sit in congested regions, so the density force pushes them apart and leaves more room for wires. RePlAce and OpenROAD's gpl use it in routability mode, with a congestion map from RUDY or a global router.

## The inflation rule

For each cell, look up the congestion ratio $r$ (demand over capacity) of its bin. If $r \le 1$, leave the cell alone. Otherwise multiply its area by an inflation factor that grows with $r$ and is capped, for example
$$f = \min(f_{max}, r^k).$$
With $f_{max} = 2.5$ and $k = 2$, a 5 um$^2$ cell in a bin with $r = 1.2$ becomes $5 \cdot 1.44 = 7.2$ um$^2$. Inflation is virtual: the cell's real size does not change, only the area the density model sees. The exponent and cap are tunable parameters; the inflated areas are recomputed whenever the congestion map is refreshed.

## Total area after inflation

Inflation adds area to the design, which the density model must absorb. For cells of 10, 9 and 4 um$^2$ in bins with ratios 0.77, 1.37 and 0.78 and $f = \min(2, r)$, only the second cell grows, to 12.33 um$^2$, so the total rises from 23 to 26.33 um$^2$. Dividing the inflated total by the region's capacity gives the new utilization; if it exceeds the target density, the placer cannot satisfy both, so implementations cap the total inflation, for example to a fraction of the available whitespace, and scale individual factors down when the budget is exceeded. That budget is what keeps inflation from simply blowing up the design.

## When inflation helps and when it does not

Inflation works on local hot spots caused by too many cells in a small area: spreading the cells spreads their wires. It works poorly on congestion caused by long nets passing through a region, since moving local cells does not reroute those through-nets, and on congestion near macros, where pin access, not cell density, is the limit. It also lengthens wires, so inflation is usually applied after the placement has spread and is reverted, or kept small, for timing-critical cells. A routability-driven placer therefore watches both the congestion map and the wirelength and timing changes, and an agent tuning it treats the cap, exponent and refresh schedule as Tier 1 parameters, validated by a real global route.

## Going deeper

Cheng, Kahng, Kang and Wang, "RePlAce" (IEEE TCAD, 2019); the OpenROAD documentation for gpl's routability-driven mode.

label: Buffering and sizing during placement
prereqs: Net delay as a function of placement
lesson:
# Buffering and sizing during placement

Placement and logic optimisation are not separate in modern flows. Long wires that placement cannot shorten are split by buffers, and gates driving heavy loads are upsized, during and right after global placement, so that timing estimates stay realistic. This placement-time optimisation, done in OpenROAD by the Resizer's repair_design and repair_timing, feeds back into where cells must go.

## Delay of a long unbuffered wire

For a driver of resistance $R_d$ driving a wire of length $L$ into a load $C_L$, the Elmore delay is $R_d(cL + C_L) + rL(cL/2 + C_L)$, whose wire term grows with $L^2$. A 2400 um wire at 0.5 ohm/um and 0.1 fF/um driven through 100 ohm into 6 fF has a driver term of $100 \cdot 246 = 24600$ ohm-fF and a wire term of $1200 \cdot 126 = 151200$ ohm-fF, 175.8 ps in total, dominated by the wire. No placement move can fix this if the two endpoints must be far apart, because they connect to logic or pins at opposite ends of the block.

## A repeater at the midpoint

Inserting a buffer of input capacitance $C_b$, output resistance $R_b$ and intrinsic delay $t_b$ at the midpoint splits the net into two stages of length $L/2$. Stage 1: $R_d(cL/2 + C_b) + r(L/2)(cL/4 + C_b)$. Stage 2: $t_b + R_b(cL/2 + C_L) + r(L/2)(cL/4 + C_L)$. Each half's wire term is a quarter of the original, so the two together are about half, at the cost of the buffer's delay and its own drive. For a 1800 um wire with $R_d = 300$ ohm and a buffer with $R_b = 150$ ohm and $t_b = 14$ ps, the delay drops from 276 ps to 183.5 ps. For short wires the buffer's intrinsic delay outweighs the saving, so buffering pays only beyond a critical length.

## Buffering and sizing inside the placement flow

Optimal buffer positions and counts on trees are found by van Ginneken's dynamic program, and gate sizing chooses drive strengths, but both need placement to know wire lengths. Flows therefore interleave: global placement, then repair of long wires, slew and capacitance violations by buffering and sizing, then incremental placement or legalization of the new cells, then timing repair. Some placers use virtual buffering, estimating buffered delays during timing-driven placement without inserting cells. The added cells need whitespace, which is one reason placement targets less than full density. A buffer inserted far from where legalization can put it loses its benefit, so buffer placement must respect density and blockages.

## Going deeper

label: The placer's core and change surface
lesson:
# The placer's core and change surface

An agent-first placer is built so that most change requests never touch its hardest code. The four-layer model splits it into an immutable core (legalization, the slot model, the numerical kernels), strategy (move sets, spreading methods, net models), parameters (weights, targets, schedules) and observation hooks (live metrics for agents). Knowing where each placer feature belongs decides how cheaply and safely it can change.

## What belongs in the placer's core

The core holds the invariants and the kernels every result depends on: the row and site slot model, the legality checker (no overlap, site alignment, rail orientation, regions), the legalizer that guarantees those properties, and the numerical kernels of global placement such as the density accumulation, the Poisson solve and the wirelength operators' interfaces. These change only for a new technology or a new kind of cell architecture, need human review, and run the full regression. Everything downstream, from CTS to routing to signoff, assumes the core's output is legal, so a bug there corrupts the flow. Keeping it small, deterministic and heavily tested is the design goal.

## Strategy, parameters and hooks

Strategy is how the placer searches: the net model (clique, star, B2B), the smooth wirelength (LSE, WA), the spreading method, the detailed-placement move set (swaps, reordering, matching), and rule plug-ins that add costs. New strategies are added as plug-ins at defined seams. Parameters are values the engine already uses: target density, overflow stopping point, timing and congestion weights, $\gamma$ schedules, inflation caps. Changing them needs no recompile. Hooks expose live state during a run, such as overflow, HPWL, density and congestion maps every N iterations, so an agent can watch, stop early or adjust parameters. Most real requests are parameter changes.

## Routing a request to a layer

A request is placed by asking what it needs that the engine does not already offer. "Use a target density of 0.65 in this region" fits an existing parameter: Tier 1. "Keep the cells of each bit-slice abutted" needs new logic that scores arrangements but does not change legality: a Tier 2 plug-in. "Let two cells overlap to save area" breaks the legality invariant: refuse or escalate. "Support rows with a new rail pattern" changes what legal means: a rare Tier 3 core change. If similar requests keep forcing core edits, a seam is missing, and adding it once turns future requests into plug-ins. Seams should take batches of cells, pass plain data and hold no hidden state, so the core stays fast and runs reproducible.

## Going deeper

The agent-first EDA notes in this curriculum, sections on the four-layer engine model and change tiers; the OpenROAD gpl and dpl documentation, for the parameters a real placer exposes.

C) The DEF reader's coordinate units

D) The rule that cells may not overlap

problems.e: How to improve a legal placement is a heuristic choice; what counts as legal is fixed.

D) Parameters
problems.a: Parameters
problems.e: It is a value the engine already uses; changing it needs no new code.

label: A placement rule as a Tier 2 plug-in
prereqs: The placer's core and change surface
Legality rules: sites, rails and regions
lesson:
# A placement rule as a Tier 2 plug-in

Customers often want placement behaviour no general placer offers: keep datapath bit-slices abutted, align regular arrays, cluster cells of one power domain near its switch. In an agent-first placer such a rule is a Tier 2 plug-in at a cost seam, which scores arrangements while the core keeps legality. "Abut regular cells" is the canonical example of this kind of plug-in.

## The seam and its context

A rule plug-in implements a narrow interface: given a batch of cells with their positions, widths, rows and tags, return a cost (and, for global placement, optionally a gradient). For "abut regular cells", the context must include a group tag per cell, so the rule knows which cells form the regular array, and row membership and x order, so it can measure gaps. The plug-in never writes positions; the core's optimiser adds its cost to the wirelength change of each candidate move and the core's legalizer still decides what is legal. Because the rule only expresses a preference, gaps remain legal, it is not a core change, and because it needs new logic, it is not a parameter.

## Computing the rule's cost

For each row, walk the members of group R in x order and add the distance from each member's right edge to the next member's left edge, whatever lies between, then multiply by the weight $\lambda$. With members at x = 0 (width 2), 5 (width 3) and 12 in one row, the gaps are 3 and 4, and with $\lambda = 2$ the cost is 14. The weight converts the rule's site units into the same scale as wirelength and is a Tier 1 parameter the user can tune. The cost should be computed incrementally, touching only the rows a move changes; recomputing every row for every candidate move makes a correct plug-in slow, and the seam should be called per batch, not per cell, so the core's inner loop stays fast.

## Proving the plug-in

A rule plug-in is accepted through golden and differential tests. Golden tests check its cost on hand-built rows with known answers, including edge cases such as one-member groups and groups split across rows. The differential test runs the placer with and without the plug-in on a regression suite: on the target design, group gaps should shrink; on every design, HPWL, overflow and timing must stay within tolerance, and legality must hold, which the core guarantees regardless of the plug-in's output. After promotion, the plug-in ships with a manifest describing the rule, its inputs and its tunable weight, so agents can select it for designs with regular datapaths. The customer's design data stays on-site; only the skill is shared.

## Going deeper

The agent-first EDA notes in this curriculum, sections on seams, extension points and golden testing; Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter 4, for the detailed-placement moves the plug-in scores.

label: Objective weights as Tier 1 configuration
prereqs: The placer's core and change surface
lesson:
# Objective weights as Tier 1 configuration

A placer's objective blends wirelength with congestion, timing and density terms through weights. Exposing those weights as configuration lets an agent answer most requests ("less congestion near the memories", "favour timing on this block") without recompiling anything. The agent's job then becomes quantitative: compute costs, compare runs and find the weight at which the preferred result changes.

## A weighted objective as configuration

Write the placement score as cost = HPWL + $\beta$ x overflow + $\gamma$ x |TNS|, or with congestion and power terms as needed. Each weight converts a metric into wirelength-equivalent units: $\beta$ = 10000 says one percent of overflow is worth 10000 um of wire. Run P with HPWL 854000 um, overflow 2% and TNS -391 ps costs $854000 + 20000 + 200 \cdot 391 = 952200$ with $\gamma$ = 200. The weights live in a configuration file or tool command, the engine reads them at start-up, and changing them is a Tier 1 change: no build, only re-runs and a QoR comparison against a baseline.

## Comparing runs

To choose between two runs, compute both costs and take the difference. Run P with HPWL 811000, overflow 4%, TNS -41 ps and run Q with 852000, 1% and -361 ps, under $\beta = 1000$ and $\gamma = 200$, cost 823200 and 925200: Q is worse by 102000, mostly from its TNS. Under a larger $\beta$ the comparison could flip, since Q has less overflow. A robust agent therefore reports not only which run wins but how sensitive the decision is to the weights, because the weights encode a judgement that the user, not the agent, should own. Runs must use the same legalizer, detailed placer and timer, or the comparison measures the tools rather than the settings.

## The break-even weight

The weight at which two runs cost the same follows from setting the costs equal. Holding $\gamma$ fixed, $\beta^* = \dfrac{C_Q - C_P}{\text{OF}_P - \text{OF}_Q}$, where $C$ is HPWL plus the TNS term. If P costs 897930 and Q 951650 without the overflow term, and their overflows are 12% and 10%, then $\beta^* = 53720/2 = 26860$: above it Q's lower overflow wins. An agent can compute such crossovers from a few runs and present them as the decision boundary, rather than silently picking a weight. If no weight setting gives what a request needs, for example a rule about specific cells, the request is not Tier 1 and needs a plug-in.

## Going deeper

The agent-first EDA notes in this curriculum, on change tiers and parameters; the OpenROAD gpl documentation for its density, timing and routability settings.

label: Golden and QoR differential tests for a placer
prereqs: The placer's core and change surface
lesson:
# Golden and QoR differential tests for a placer

No change to a placer, whether a parameter, a plug-in or a core edit, should be promoted on faith. Golden tests prove that kernels compute what they should; QoR differential tests compare the changed placer with a baseline across a regression suite and prove that only the intended metrics moved, by the intended amounts. Writing the gates precisely is what makes agent-generated changes safe to accept.

## Golden tests for placer kernels

Golden tests check deterministic pieces against known answers: HPWL of hand-built nets, B2B weights, density of a small bin grid, the Abacus result on a three-cell row, the legality checker on legal and illegal examples, and the incremental wirelength delta against full recomputation for random moves. They run in seconds, so the harness runs them after every edit. For a change at a seam, the plug-in's own golden tests join the suite. Determinism is a precondition: with fixed seeds and ordered reductions, the same input must give bit-identical output, otherwise a golden mismatch cannot be told apart from noise.

## Measuring QoR change

A QoR comparison runs the baseline and the changed placer on the same designs with the same downstream flow and reports metric changes. The basic number is the percent change: HPWL from 458000 to 455000 um is $-0.66\%$. A suite summary uses the geometric mean of new-over-baseline ratios, which treats a 1% change on a small design and on a large one equally and keeps one large design from dominating; for ratios 0.99, 1.01 and 0.97, the geometric mean is about 0.9899. Metrics include HPWL, overflow, legalization displacement, routed wirelength and DRC count where available, timing (WNS, TNS) and runtime, since a QoR gain that doubles runtime may not be acceptable.

## Promotion gates

A gate turns measurements into a decision. A typical one: on every regression design, HPWL may grow by at most 1% over baseline, overflow must stay at most 0.1, legality must hold, and runtime may grow by at most 10%. The change is blocked if any design fails, and the report lists which designs and metrics broke. For a targeted change, such as a rule plug-in, the gate also checks that the intended effect appears on the target design. Gates should be strict enough to catch regressions and loose enough to tolerate run-to-run noise, which is measured by running the baseline several times. Every promoted change is versioned and reversible, so a regression found later can be traced and rolled back.

## Going deeper

The agent-first EDA notes in this curriculum, section on verification of engine changes; the OpenROAD-flow-scripts metrics and regression documentation.

problems.q: A placer change is run on a reference design: baseline HPWL 628000 um, new HPWL 633652 um. What is the HPWL change, in percent (negative is better)? Round to 2 decimal places.
A placer change is run on a reference design: baseline HPWL 268000 um, new HPWL 267464 um. What is the HPWL change, in percent (negative is better)? Round to 2 decimal places.

label: Fast placement inside a modeling loop
prereqs: Fast and accurate engines in a modeling loop
lesson:
# Fast placement inside a modeling loop

Placement exists in fast and accurate forms: a GPU global placer with loose stopping rules and RUDY congestion, versus full global and detailed placement followed by global routing. An agent exploring floorplans or parameters runs the fast version in a loop, uses its metrics and their error to decide which candidates deserve the accurate version, and bases final decisions only on accurate results.

## What the fast placer trades away

A fast placer stops at a higher overflow, uses coarser bins, skips or shortens detailed placement and estimates congestion with RUDY instead of a router. It returns HPWL, overflow and a congestion map in a fraction of the time, with a known error relative to the accurate flow. That error must be measured, not assumed: run both on a sample of designs and record the spread of the ratio, for example HPWL within about 3%. The fast placer must also be deterministic and seedable, so that differences between candidates come from the candidates rather than from noise, and its error should be re-measured whenever the design family changes.

## Deciding what to run accurately

Given fast estimates and an error band of $\pm e$, a candidate can be discarded only if even its optimistic value, estimate times $(1 - e)$, is worse than the best candidate's pessimistic value, best estimate times $(1 + e)$. With estimates 934, 910, 905, 990, 1059, 952, 1048 and 944 mm and $e = 2\%$, the best pessimistic value is 923.1 and only candidates whose optimistic value is at most that survive: 905, 910 and 934, three candidates for the accurate placer. If many candidates survive, the error band is too wide for the decision and the agent needs a better fast model or more accurate runs. Metric variance across seeds plays the same role as the error band.

## Pitfalls of the loop

An agent rewarded on fast-placer metrics can learn to exploit the fast model's blind spots, for example floorplans whose RUDY estimate looks clean but whose real routing congests near macros, a form of reward hacking. Guards include adding routability terms that correlate with the accurate flow, periodic accurate audits of chosen candidates, and making final decisions only from accurate results. Speed shifts the bottleneck: when global placement takes a minute, I/O, legalization and evaluation dominate, so the loop is only as fast as its slowest stage. The fast placer, its error model and the selection rule together form a skill whose manifest should state when its estimates can be trusted.

## Going deeper

The agent-first EDA notes in this curriculum, section on fast and accurate engines in a continuous loop; Lin et al., "DREAMPlace" (DAC 2019), on GPU placement speed.

problems.q:
What does a fast placer typically trade away to run inside a modeling loop?

A) Legality of the netlist

B) The ability to read DEF

C) Determinism, always

D) Accuracy: fewer iterations, coarser bins or skipped detailed placement
problems.a: Accuracy: fewer iterations, coarser bins or skipped detailed placement
problems.e: Fast modes stop earlier and approximate more, giving estimates rather than final QoR.

problems.q:

problems.e: Fast results guide decisions; accurate runs confirm the chosen candidates.
